newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Dubai-based Dolphin tries to deflect S.African row.
newsitem.headline: Dubai-based Dolphin tries to deflect S.African row.

text.p: A Dubai-based multinational company which wants to gain commercial control over nature reserves in South Africa responded to critics on Wednesday, saying its motives were pure.

Environmentalists have poured scorn on the deal signed by the Dolphin Group with the state-owned Mpumalanga Parks Board last November -- and land claims by blacks who say that they were deprived of territory under apartheid could yet derail it.
The Dolphin Group's Kenyan-born chief executive, Ketan Somaia, said in the first public reaction to criticism: "It is unfortunate that there has been ill-informed comment."

"We are confident that we will contribute much needed capital, skills and infrastructure for the benefit of South Africans," he said in a statement issued through a South African public relations company.
The reserves in question lie in Mpumalanga province, home also to South Africa's vast Kruger National Park. Dolphin plans to inject 400 million rand ($84 million) into the project.

Criticism centres on the secrecy which allowed the deal to be signed without prior public debate, a clause apparently allowing profits to be accrued abroad and charges that the parks board had sacrificed too much control to Dolphin.
Somaia said the secrecy clause in the contract was "no more than the standard confidentiality provision".

Dolphin had also only leased the rights to the reserves "for a period long enough to enable it to make a realistic commercial return", and had not asked the parks board to abdicate its duty to protect the environment, he said.
Under the deal, Dolphin takes commercial rights to five tourism areas in return for bankrolling the parks board's accumulated deficit for 50 years.
There is also an agreement that blacks living on the borders of the reserves will be given a 20 percent share of development companies to be set up in the target areas.
But these communities could still scupper the project if their land claims, pending against two reserves, succeed. No date has yet been set for the claims to be settled.
